## Windows

On Windows the backend is AppContainer, as Windows 10 version 1809 and later give, needing no administrator rights. Each run gets an AppContainer of its own, made with `CreateAppContainerProfile` and named `Suspense.<profile>.<run id>`, so two runs never share an identity and one run's grants never reach another's; it is deleted with `DeleteAppContainerProfile` once the run is over. An AppContainer's process reaches no file in the user's folders or the project unless that path's access list names its identity, so the filesystem boundary is the access lists, checked by the kernel on every open, whatever program opens the file.
Before the run, each path the policy grants is given an access entry for the run's AppContainer SID, with `SetNamedSecurityInfoW` on the path's handle, opened without following reparse points: read and execute for read-only grants, modify for read-write ones, inherited by everything beneath it. A denied path is never beneath a grant, as the policy's expansion ensures, so no inherited entry can reach it; where the expansion is too deep to make, the run is refused, as a contradiction. The entries are added with the AppContainer's SID alone, never the user's or any group's, so they widen nothing for any other process. Each entry added is written first to a ledger in Suspense's data directory, with its path and the SID, so it is always removed after the run, however it ended, and at the next launch for any run the application didn't see end, as after a crash: no grant is ever left in place.
The harness is started with `CreateProcessW` given the AppContainer's security capabilities in its attribute list, `internetClient` among them so the harness can reach its model service, and nothing else: no `privateNetworkClientServer`, no broad file capabilities such as documents or removable storage. The process is created suspended, assigned to a job object of the run's own with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` and breakaway forbidden, and only then resumed, so nothing it starts can leave the job or the AppContainer, and closing the job ends them all. Its standard input, output, and error are pipes the application makes, the only handles it inherits, listed explicitly with `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST`, and it starts without a console window, as the [Application](../application/index.md#application) says.
What the harness and its tools need from outside the project is granted read-only by path, found on the host as the application finds

### Programs

the harness's installation, Node.js where the harness runs

on it, git, the language toolchains, as MSVC, the Windows SDKs, and `.cargo` and `.rustup`, and PowerShell's modules. The harness's own folder in the user's profile, as `.claude`, its caches, the toolchains' caches builds write to, and a temporary folder of the run's own, given as TEMP and TMP, are granted read-write. The system's own folders, `C:\Windows` and `C:\Program Files`, are readable by AppContainers as Windows installs them, through the ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES group, and need no grant; nothing is ever granted to that group, nor to ALL RESTRICTED APPLICATION PACKAGES, since it would reach every AppContainer. A path the user can't change the access list of, as one owned by another account, can't be granted, and a run that needs it doesn't start, saying which path.
Neither a job object nor a restricted token alone is taken as a filesystem boundary; the AppContainer is. The named pipe the piton shim talks over is made with a security descriptor naming only the run's AppContainer SID and the user, so no other process can open it. Where an AppContainer can't be made, a capability can't be given, a grant can't be added or recorded, or the Windows version is older than 1809, the run doesn't start, saying which, as failing closed says, and the Status card in the settings says the sandbox can't run here and why.
Its tests run on the Windows runner as on the others, as the verification says, and check besides that a file the run is denied can't be opened through a junction, a symbolic link, a hard link, an 8.3 short name, or an alternate data stream, that a process the run starts can't open a process outside its job, and that no access entry for a run's SID remains once it is over.

## Channels

The sandbox closes what reaches the filesystem by another route: every file descriptor or handle but its standard input, output, and error, and the piton channel, is closed before the harness runs, so none open on a denied file can be inherited; on Linux and macOS, Unix sockets outside the run's grants can't be connected to, so no local service, as an SSH agent, a Docker socket, or another editor, can be asked to read the project for it; and on Windows, the run's identity can't open named pipes or services but its own. The account's connectors are already never given to a run, as the [HarnessIntegration](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says.
What remains outside the enforcement boundary is said plainly, in the sandbox's documentation and in the Sandbox section of the settings, never claimed as protected: the network, through which a run could fetch the project from a remote repository or a forge it is published to; the harness's own service, which holds what was sent to it in earlier conversations of the same lane; and the clipboard. These are for the user to decide on, and the sandbox doesn't pretend to close them.

## Linux

On Linux the backend is Landlock, applied in the child process just before it runs the harness's program, with `no_new_privs` set first, so it is never applied to Suspense itself and needs no root. It restricts reading, writing, executing, renaming, linking, and truncating, by an allow-list of paths opened as file descriptors, and the restriction survives every exec and is inherited by every child. It needs Landlock ABI 3 or later, as Linux 6.2 gives, so that truncation is covered too, and ABI 6 or later, as Linux 6.12 gives, to scope Unix sockets; on a kernel that has an older ABI, the Unix socket scoping is left out and said to be, and on one with no Landlock, or older than ABI 3, nothing runs, as failing closed says. Nothing else is used: no namespaces or seccomp, unless a concrete part of the policy can't be enforced without them.

## Macos

On macOS the backend is Seatbelt: a sandbox profile generated from the policy, in the sandbox profile language, applied to the child as it starts, as `sandbox-exec` does, inherited by every process it starts, and needing no administrator rights. It denies by default and allows reading and writing only the policy's paths, the system's own, and what Xcode and its command-line tools, `xcodebuild`, the SDKs, and their caches and DerivedData need, which the backend grants by their resolved paths. Seatbelt's interface is deprecated by Apple and undocumented in parts, as the sandbox's documentation says, and the backend's behaviour is tested on each macOS the releases are built for, never assumed from a profile that applied.

## Windows

On Windows the backend is AppContainer, as Windows 10 version 1809 and later give, needing no administrator rights. Each run gets an AppContainer of its own, made with `CreateAppContainerProfile` and named `Suspense.<profile>.<run id>`, so two runs never share an identity and one run's grants never reach another's; it is deleted with `DeleteAppContainerProfile` once the run is over. An AppContainer's process reaches no file in the user's folders or the project unless that path's access list names its identity, so the filesystem boundary is the access lists, checked by the kernel on every open, whatever program opens the file.
Before the run, each path the policy grants is given an access entry for the run's AppContainer SID, with `SetNamedSecurityInfoW` on the path's handle, opened without following reparse points: read and execute for read-only grants, modify for read-write ones, inherited by everything beneath it. A denied path is never beneath a grant, as the policy's expansion ensures, so no inherited entry can reach it; where the expansion is too deep to make, the run is refused, as a contradiction. The entries are added with the AppContainer's SID alone, never the user's or any group's, so they widen nothing for any other process. Each entry added is written first to a ledger in Suspense's data directory, with its path and the SID, so it is always removed after the run, however it ended, and at the next launch for any run the application didn't see end, as after a crash: no grant is ever left in place.
The harness is started with `CreateProcessW` given the AppContainer's security capabilities in its attribute list, `internetClient` among them so the harness can reach its model service, and nothing else: no `privateNetworkClientServer`, no broad file capabilities such as documents or removable storage. The process is created suspended, assigned to a job object of the run's own with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` and breakaway forbidden, and only then resumed, so nothing it starts can leave the job or the AppContainer, and closing the job ends them all. Its standard input, output, and error are pipes the application makes, the only handles it inherits, listed explicitly with `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST`, and it starts without a console window, as the [Application](../application/index.md#application) says.
What the harness and its tools need from outside the project is granted read-only by path, found on the host as the application finds

### Programs

the harness's installation, Node.js where the harness runs

on it, git, the language toolchains, as MSVC, the Windows SDKs, and `.cargo` and `.rustup`, and PowerShell's modules. The harness's own folder in the user's profile, as `.claude`, its caches, the toolchains' caches builds write to, and a temporary folder of the run's own, given as TEMP and TMP, are granted read-write. The system's own folders, `C:\Windows` and `C:\Program Files`, are readable by AppContainers as Windows installs them, through the ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES group, and need no grant; nothing is ever granted to that group, nor to ALL RESTRICTED APPLICATION PACKAGES, since it would reach every AppContainer. A path the user can't change the access list of, as one owned by another account, can't be granted, and a run that needs it doesn't start, saying which path.
Neither a job object nor a restricted token alone is taken as a filesystem boundary; the AppContainer is. The named pipe the piton shim talks over is made with a security descriptor naming only the run's AppContainer SID and the user, so no other process can open it. Where an AppContainer can't be made, a capability can't be given, a grant can't be added or recorded, or the Windows version is older than 1809, the run doesn't start, saying which, as failing closed says, and the Status card in the settings says the sandbox can't run here and why.
Its tests run on the Windows runner as on the others, as the verification says, and check besides that a file the run is denied can't be opened through a junction, a symbolic link, a hard link, an 8.3 short name, or an alternate data stream, that a process the run starts can't open a process outside its job, and that no access entry for a run's SID remains once it is over.

## Compatibility

Normal native development works inside each profile: in the Code profile, `cargo build` and `cargo test`, git through the filtered repository, shell scripts, and the platform's compilers on Linux; native builds, the Xcode command-line tools, and `xcodebuild` on macOS; PowerShell, MSVC, Cargo, and the native build tools on Windows; each reaching the system, the SDKs, the toolchains, their caches, and the run's temporary directory, and none reaching what the profile denies. Project restrictions are never widened to make a command succeed: a build that needs a denied path fails, saying the sandbox refused it, and naming the path.

## Verification

The sandbox is tested on each platform, by the tests the [EdgeReleases](../edge-releases/index.md#edge-releases) run, against what the operating system actually does, never a mocked decision: a harness of hostile commands runs inside each profile in a temporary project of its own, and asserts that in the Code profile the code can be read and written and the compiled reference read, while the spec can be neither read nor written; that the Spec profile is the same the other way round; and that none of these can get past it: a shell, Python, Node.js, a Rust or C++ program run inside, a child of a child, `..` paths, symbolic links, junctions, hard links, renames across the boundary, inherited descriptors, a race swapping a path, and git, whose `show`, `log`, `cat-file`, and `stash` show nothing denied. A policy the platform can't enforce refuses to run, and the representative native builds above still work. A platform where any of these can't be tested, or fails, is said so in the documentation, never released as protected.

## Documentation

The sandbox's guarantees and limits are written down in the repository, in `SANDBOX.md` beside the module: what each backend enforces on which versions of each platform, what remains outside it, as the channels say, which escape routes were tested and how, and the approach chosen against the implementations that were weighed, `nolabs-ai/nono`, `openai/codex`'s native sandboxes, `anthropics/sandbox-runtime`, `eugene1g/agent-safehouse`, and `LeGambiArt/arapuca`: their licences, maturity, dependencies, and what each really enforces, and why the parts reused were reused and the rest weren't. An existing, auditable Rust library is used for a backend wherever one does what the policy needs, as the `landlock` crate on Linux, rather than writing the system's own security interfaces again, and no large framework is brought in for it.

## Examples

The repository holds examples beside the module, one per profile, as a small program that runs a command under the Code profile and one under the Spec profile for a sample project, so the sandbox can be tried and its behaviour seen apart from the rest of the application.

On Windows the backend is AppContainer, as Windows 10 version 1809 and later give, needing no administrator rights. Each run gets an AppContainer of its own, made with `CreateAppContainerProfile` and named `Suspense.<profile>.<run id>`, so two runs never share an identity and one run's grants never reach another's; it is deleted with `DeleteAppContainerProfile` once the run is over. An AppContainer's process reaches no file in the user's folders or the project unless that path's access list names its identity, so the filesystem boundary is the access lists, checked by the kernel on every open, whatever program opens the file.
Before the run, each path the policy grants is given an access entry for the run's AppContainer SID, with `SetNamedSecurityInfoW` on the path's handle, opened without following reparse points: read and execute for read-only grants, modify for read-write ones, inherited by everything beneath it. A denied path is never beneath a grant, as the policy's expansion ensures, so no inherited entry can reach it; where the expansion is too deep to make, the run is refused, as a contradiction. The entries are added with the AppContainer's SID alone, never the user's or any group's, so they widen nothing for any other process. Each entry added is written first to a ledger in Suspense's data directory, with its path and the SID, so it is always removed after the run, however it ended, and at the next launch for any run the application didn't see end, as after a crash: no grant is ever left in place.
The harness is started with `CreateProcessW` given the AppContainer's security capabilities in its attribute list, `internetClient` among them so the harness can reach its model service, and nothing else: no `privateNetworkClientServer`, no broad file capabilities such as documents or removable storage. The process is created suspended, assigned to a job object of the run's own with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` and breakaway forbidden, and only then resumed, so nothing it starts can leave the job or the AppContainer, and closing the job ends them all. Its standard input, output, and error are pipes the application makes, the only handles it inherits, listed explicitly with `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST`, and it starts without a console window, as the [Application](../application/index.md#application) says.
What the harness and its tools need from outside the project is granted read-only by path, found on the host as the application finds

### Programs

the harness's installation, Node.js where the harness runs

on it, git, the language toolchains, as MSVC, the Windows SDKs, and `.cargo` and `.rustup`, and PowerShell's modules. The harness's own folder in the user's profile, as `.claude`, its caches, the toolchains' caches builds write to, and a temporary folder of the run's own, given as TEMP and TMP, are granted read-write. The system's own folders, `C:\Windows` and `C:\Program Files`, are readable by AppContainers as Windows installs them, through the ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES group, and need no grant; nothing is ever granted to that group, nor to ALL RESTRICTED APPLICATION PACKAGES, since it would reach every AppContainer. A path the user can't change the access list of, as one owned by another account, can't be granted, and a run that needs it doesn't start, saying which path.
Neither a job object nor a restricted token alone is taken as a filesystem boundary; the AppContainer is. The named pipe the piton shim talks over is made with a security descriptor naming only the run's AppContainer SID and the user, so no other process can open it. Where an AppContainer can't be made, a capability can't be given, a grant can't be added or recorded, or the Windows version is older than 1809, the run doesn't start, saying which, as failing closed says, and the Status card in the settings says the sandbox can't run here and why.
Its tests run on the Windows runner as on the others, as the verification says, and check besides that a file the run is denied can't be opened through a junction, a symbolic link, a hard link, an 8.3 short name, or an alternate data stream, that a process the run starts can't open a process outside its job, and that no access entry for a run's SID remains once it is over.

## Compatibility

Normal native development works inside each profile: in the Code profile, `cargo build` and `cargo test`, git through the filtered repository, shell scripts, and the platform's compilers on Linux; native builds, the Xcode command-line tools, and `xcodebuild` on macOS; PowerShell, MSVC, Cargo, and the native build tools on Windows; each reaching the system, the SDKs, the toolchains, their caches, and the run's temporary directory, and none reaching what the profile denies. Project restrictions are never widened to make a command succeed: a build that needs a denied path fails, saying the sandbox refused it, and naming the path.

## Verification

The sandbox is tested on each platform, by the tests the [EdgeReleases](../edge-releases/index.md#edge-releases) run, against what the operating system actually does, never a mocked decision: a harness of hostile commands runs inside each profile in a temporary project of its own, and asserts that in the Code profile the code can be read and written and the compiled reference read, while the spec can be neither read nor written; that the Spec profile is the same the other way round; and that none of these can get past it: a shell, Python, Node.js, a Rust or C++ program run inside, a child of a child, `..` paths, symbolic links, junctions, hard links, renames across the boundary, inherited descriptors, a race swapping a path, and git, whose `show`, `log`, `cat-file`, and `stash` show nothing denied. A policy the platform can't enforce refuses to run, and the representative native builds above still work. A platform where any of these can't be tested, or fails, is said so in the documentation, never released as protected.

## Documentation

The sandbox's guarantees and limits are written down in the repository, in `SANDBOX.md` beside the module: what each backend enforces on which versions of each platform, what remains outside it, as the channels say, which escape routes were tested and how, and the approach chosen against the implementations that were weighed, `nolabs-ai/nono`, `openai/codex`'s native sandboxes, `anthropics/sandbox-runtime`, `eugene1g/agent-safehouse`, and `LeGambiArt/arapuca`: their licences, maturity, dependencies, and what each really enforces, and why the parts reused were reused and the rest weren't. An existing, auditable Rust library is used for a backend wherever one does what the policy needs, as the `landlock` crate on Linux, rather than writing the system's own security interfaces again, and no large framework is brought in for it.

## Examples

The repository holds examples beside the module, one per profile, as a small program that runs a command under the Code profile and one under the Spec profile for a sample project, so the sandbox can be tried and its behaviour seen apart from the rest of the application.

# Suspense's sandbox

Every harness run Suspense starts — Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode, and everything that run starts in turn — runs natively on the host under a filesystem policy the operating system enforces. A **Code** run can't read or change the spec's source. A **Spec** run can't read or change the code. There is no container, VM, or WSL. The module is `src/sandbox/`.

## Guarantees

| | Linux (Landlock) | macOS (Seatbelt) | Windows (AppContainer) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Status | **Enforced and tested** | Implemented, **untested** | **Not built: runs refuse** |
| Read / write / list / execute denied outside grants | yes (ABI ≥ 3) | yes, by profile | — |
| Truncate | yes (ABI ≥ 3) | yes | — |
| Rename / link across the boundary | yes (`Refer`, ABI ≥ 2) | yes | — |
| Inherited by every descendant, can't be lifted | yes (`no_new_privs`, Landlock domain) | yes | — |
| Abstract Unix sockets and signals scoped to the run | ABI ≥ 6 | — | — |
| Connecting to path-named Unix sockets outside grants | ABI ≥ 9 (`ResolveUnix`, Linux 7.1) | **no**: the profile allows `network*`, which includes Unix sockets | — |
| Inherited file descriptors closed | yes (`close_range(CLOEXEC)`) | inherits the parent's close-on-exec only | — |
| Fails closed | yes: no Landlock, or ABI < 3, means no run starts | yes, if `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` is missing | always, until it's built |

**On Linux** the ruleset is built in Suspense, with every granted path opened as a descriptor and checked against the identity it had when the policy was compiled. It is applied in the child just before `exec`, with `no_new_privs` set first. Nothing is applied to Suspense itself, and no root is needed. Landlock has no notion of "deny inside an allow". So the policy is compiled to an allow-list: a granted folder that holds a denied path is expanded into grants of its other entries, level by level.

**On macOS** a Seatbelt profile (`(deny default)` + explicit `file-read*`/`file-write*` subpaths + trailing `deny` rules for denied paths) is generated per run and the harness is started through `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -p`. Apple has deprecated `sandbox-exec`, and its profile language is undocumented. It still works on current macOS and is what Codex, Chrome and agent-safehouse rely on. This backend **has not been run on a Mac yet**: until it passes `cargo test sandbox::` there, treat macOS as unprotected.

**On Windows** the AppContainer backend the spec describes is **not implemented**. Every run that needs a sandbox — which is every task and question — fails before it starts, saying so. Nothing is run unrestricted. This is the main open item.

## Profiles

Built by the application from the run's kind, never chosen by the run. The full rules are in the Sandbox spec's profiles section.

- **Spec**: the spec roots, the harness directory and `.piton` read-write; `piton.config.pi` read-only; the code roots denied unless the project lets Spec runs read them, when they're read-only.
- **Question**: the code, the spec, the harness directory and the config, all read-only.
- **Freeform**: the whole project, with the real `.git`; `.suspense` excluded.
- **Bare** (commit notes, titles, commit messages): nothing in the project.

Every profile also gets:

- its attached files, read-only;
- its understanding file, read-write;
- the two fluency files, read-only;
- the project's top-level `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` and `.mcp.json`, read-only;

content.text:
Sandboxing now works on Windows in theory. It builds for the Windows target with no errors or lint warnings, but it hasn't run on a Windows machine yet, so treat Windows as unprotected until the Windows tests pass there.

**How it works:**
- **One AppContainer per run**, named `Suspense.<profile>.<run>`. A small launcher (`suspense --sandbox-launch`) creates it, gives each allowed path an access entry for that run only, and records each entry in a ledger before adding it.
- **Starting the harness:** it starts paused, with only internet access, only its three standard handles, no console window, and inside a job that kills everything when it closes and that nothing can leave. Only then is it resumed.
- **Cleanup:** afterwards the launcher removes the entries and the AppContainer. Anything left after a crash is removed at the next launch.
- **Version check:** the Status card shows "AppContainer: files and named pipes", or says the sandbox can't run on Windows older than 1809 (build 17763).
- **The `piton` command** goes through a named pipe that only the run and the user can open. On the run's PATH it's a `piton.cmd`.
- **Programs outside the project:** the folders of Node, git, PowerShell, MSVC and Cargo can be read, and the npm, pip and Visual Studio caches can be written.
- **Tests:** I added Windows-only tests for junctions, symbolic links, hard links, short (8.3) names, hidden file streams, reaching a process outside the job, and access entries left behind. `SANDBOX.md` is updated to match.

**Bug fixed along the way:** the settings Test button ran its 12 checks through `sh`, which doesn't exist on Windows. Every check would have failed to start and been counted as "refused", so it would have reported a false 12 of 12. The checks now have `cmd` versions for Windows.

**Where I didn't do exactly what the spec says:**
- **Low-integrity label:** the spec says the access entries widen nothing for any other process. But an AppContainer runs at low integrity, and I believe (not yet confirmed on Windows) that it can't write to normal files even when allowed to. So folders the run may write are also marked low integrity for the run's duration. While the run lasts, another low-integrity program of the same user could also write there. The label is recorded in the ledger and removed with the access entries.
- **By path, not by handle:** the spec says to set access through an open handle that doesn't follow links. I set it by path and refuse any path that is a link or junction. That leaves a small gap between the check and the change.

**Checked on Linux:** the Linux build is clean and the 16 sandbox tests still pass.

I also wrote the constraints file after I had already started on `src/sandbox/windows.rs`, not before.
